title: Structural Dissociation
subtitle: A clinical model of divided action systems
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating structural dissociation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain structural dissociation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in structural dissociation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to structural dissociation.

sections.explainSimply: Structural dissociation conceptualises trauma-related divisions between everyday functioning and defensive action systems.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: It may aid formulation in complex presentations, but it is a theoretical clinical model rather than an established anatomical partition.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Use carefully alongside differential diagnosis, cultural formulation and assessment of memory, identity, psychosis and neurological causes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of structural dissociation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need structural dissociation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not reify parts as literal brain structures or suggest identities.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use structural dissociation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses structural dissociation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not reify parts as literal brain structures or suggest identities. Evidence classification: theoretical model; practitioner use.
